title: Ἀπιστία Εὐμαίου
about: Odysseus, fed and given a cup of wine, asks Eumaeus who bought him, in case he has heard of such a master. Eumaeus answers that no wandering stranger has ever been believed about Odysseus: beggars lie to his lady for a cloak and a tunic, and for him the master is dead, his bones in the sand or the sea. Odysseus, hiding who he is, swears by Zeus, the table and the hearth that Odysseus will come home within the year, and asks to be rewarded with clothes when he does. Eumaeus will have none of it. He grieves for Odysseus and for Telemachus, who has gone to Pylos and is waylaid on his return by the suitors, and then asks the stranger for his own story, who he is and how he came to Ithaca. Odysseus answers that a year would not be long enough to tell all he has suffered, but that he will tell it exactly.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὁ δ’ ἐνδυκέως κρέα τ’ ἤσθιε πῖνέ τε οἶνον
ἁρπαλέως ἀκέων, κακὰ δὲ μνηστῆρσι φύτευεν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and he, kindly, both meat ate and drank wine
greedily, in silence, and evils for the suitors he was planting.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Odysseus ate the meat with a will and drank the wine, eagerly and in silence, while he devised evil for the suitors.
sentences.n: The speaker of the last lines was Eumaeus; with ὁ δ’ ‘but he’ the subject turns to Odysseus, who eats while Eumaeus has finished. ὣς φάθ’ is ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’, elided before the rough breathing of ὁ (τ becomes θ). ἐνδυκέως is kept as the house ‘kindly’ in l; said of eating it means something like ‘assiduously, attentively’, so i says ‘with a will’. ἁρπαλέως is ‘greedily, eagerly’. ἀκέων is an adjective of participle form, ‘silent’, here ‘in silence’. κακὰ … φύτευεν: φυτεύω is ‘plant’, so the harm is a crop he is planting; the imperfect shows him at it as he eats. μνηστῆρσι is a dative plural, ‘for the suitors’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δείπνησε καὶ ἤραρε θυμὸν ἐδωδῇ,
καί οἱ πλησάμενος δῶκε σκύφον, ᾧ περ ἔπινεν,
οἴνου ἐνίπλειον·
sentences.i: But when he had eaten his fill and satisfied his heart with food, Eumaeus filled the cup he drank from himself and gave it to him, brimming with wine;
sentences.n: The subject changes without being named: δείπνησε is Odysseus, who has finished eating, and δῶκε is Eumaeus, who gives him the cup. δείπνησε is the aorist of δειπνέω ‘take a meal’, and ἤραρε θυμὸν ἐδωδῇ ‘fitted his heart with food’ is a stock line for a satisfied appetite. πλησάμενος is the aorist middle participle of πίμπλημι ‘fill’; οἱ is ‘to him’; σκύφον is a drinking cup. ᾧ περ ἔπινεν is ‘from which he himself drank’: ᾧ is the relative, the subject of ἔπινεν is Eumaeus, and περ adds ‘the very cup’. ἐνίπλειον ‘full’ takes the genitive οἴνου ‘of wine’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐδέξατο, χαῖρε δὲ θυμῷ,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
and he received it, and was glad in his heart,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Odysseus took it, glad at heart, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is Odysseus again: ἐδέξατο is the aorist of δέχομαι ‘receive’, and χαῖρε δὲ θυμῷ is ‘was glad in his heart’. μιν is ‘him’, that is Eumaeus; the pronoun is not the article. φωνήσας is ‘having raised his voice’. The last line is the stock introduction to a speech: ἔπεα πτερόεντα are ‘winged words’, translated every time, and προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλε, τίς γάρ σε πρίατο κτεάτεσσιν ἑοῖσιν,
ὧδε μάλ’ ἀφνειὸς καὶ καρτερὸς ὡς ἀγορεύεις;
sentences.l:
“O friend, for who bought you with his own possessions,
so very rich and strong, as you say?
sentences.i: “My friend, who was it that bought you with his own wealth, a man as rich and strong as you say?
sentences.n: Odysseus asks who Eumaeus’ master was, and the question is addressed to Eumaeus. ὦ φίλε is ‘my friend’ (‘O friend’ in l). πρίατο is an aorist ‘bought’, with no augment. κτεάτεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσιν of κτέατα ‘possessions’, and ἑοῖσιν is the possessive ‘his own’ (the dative plural of ἑός), not a relative: the buyer paid from his own wealth. ἀφνειός ‘rich’ and καρτερός ‘strong’ (the same word as κρατερός) agree with τίς, so the man asked about is ‘so very rich and strong’. ὡς ἀγορεύεις is ‘as you say’. The question ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: φῆς δ’ αὐτὸν φθίσθαι Ἀγαμέμνονος εἵνεκα τιμῆς.
sentences.l: And you say that he perished for the sake of Agamemnon’s honour.
sentences.i: And you say he died for the sake of Agamemnon’s honour.
sentences.n: φῆς is ‘you say’ (the second person of φημί), with the infinitive φθίσθαι, the aorist middle of φθίνω ‘perish’; αὐτόν is ‘him’, the master, not ‘himself’. Ἀγαμέμνονος εἵνεκα τιμῆς is ‘for the sake of Agamemnon’s honour’, with εἵνεκα standing between the two genitives and governing τιμῆς; Eumaeus had said earlier that his master went to Troy for this cause.

sentences.t: εἰπέ μοι, αἴ κέ ποθι γνώω τοιοῦτον ἐόντα.
sentences.l: Tell me, in case somewhere I may know him, being such.
sentences.i: Tell me, in case I know of such a man somewhere.
sentences.n: εἰπέ is the aorist imperative ‘tell’. αἴ κε is εἰ κε ‘if perhaps, in case’, and ποθι is the enclitic ‘somewhere’ (Attic που). γνώω is the aorist subjunctive of γιγνώσκω ‘come to know, recognise’ with a long vowel (Attic γνῶ). τοιοῦτον ἐόντα is ‘him being such’: ἐόντα is Homeric for ὄντα, and the master is described as the sort of man Eumaeus has said he was.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς γάρ που τό γε οἶδε καὶ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι,
εἴ κέ μιν ἀγγείλαιμι ἰδών·
sentences.l:
For Zeus doubtless this at least knows, and the other immortal gods,
whether I could report him, having seen him;
sentences.i: For Zeus doubtless knows, and the other immortal gods, whether I could bring word of him, having seen him;
sentences.n: The sentence says that only the gods know whether the speaker could bring word of that man, having seen him. που is ‘doubtless, I suppose’; τό γε is ‘that at least’, pointing ahead to the clause with εἰ. ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι is ‘the other immortal gods’. εἴ κέ μιν ἀγγείλαιμι ἰδών is an indirect question with κε and the optative, ‘whether I could report him’: ἀγγείλαιμι is the aorist optative of ἀγγέλλω, and ἰδών the aorist participle of ὁράω, ‘having seen (him)’. The unit ends at the ano teleia after ἰδών.

sentences.t: ἐπὶ πολλὰ δ’ ἀλήθην.
sentences.l: and over many places I wandered.”
sentences.i: and I have wandered far and wide.”
sentences.n: ἀλήθην is the aorist passive of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’ without the augment (Attic ἠλήθην). ἐπὶ πολλά is ‘over many places’, with πολλά neuter plural; δ’ is δέ ‘and’. This ends Odysseus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα συβώτης, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l: Him then answered the swineherd, chief of men:
sentences.i: Then the swineherd, chief of men, answered him:
sentences.n: The house reply-formula: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘then he answered him’, with τόν a pronoun (‘him’) and ἠμείβετ’ the elided imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. συβώτης is ‘swineherd’ (σῦς ‘swine’ and the root of βόσκω ‘feed, tend’). ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν ‘chief of men’ is a stock epithet, translated every time even though it sits oddly on a swineherd.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον, οὔ τις κεῖνον ἀνὴρ ἀλαλήμενος ἐλθὼν
ἀγγέλλων πείσειε γυναῖκά τε καὶ φίλον υἱόν,
ἀλλ’ ἄλλως κομιδῆς κεχρημένοι ἄνδρες ἀλῆται
ψεύδοντ’, οὐδ’ ἐθέλουσιν ἀληθέα μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.l:
“Old man, no wanderer, having come
reporting him, could persuade his wife and dear son,
but idly, men in need of care, vagrants,
lie, and are not willing to tell true things.
sentences.i: “Old man, no wanderer who came with news of him would persuade his wife and dear son; vagrants in need of care lie idly and will not tell the truth.
sentences.n: Eumaeus explains why he does not believe stories of Odysseus’ return. ὦ γέρον is ‘old man’. ἀλαλήμενος is the perfect participle of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’; ἀγγέλλων ‘reporting’ has κεῖνον ‘that man’ as its object. πείσειε is an optative without κε, ‘would persuade’. ἄλλως is ‘idly, to no purpose’ (its first sense is ‘otherwise’). κομιδῆς κεχρημένοι is ‘needing care’: κομιδή is ‘tending, looking after’ and κεχρημένοι is a perfect participle meaning ‘needing’, with the genitive. ἀλῆται is ‘vagrants’. ψεύδοντ’ is ψεύδονται ‘lie’, and ἐθέλουσιν is ‘they are willing’. Four lines run to one full stop, so the unit is not cut.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κ’ ἀλητεύων Ἰθάκης ἐς δῆμον ἵκηται,
ἐλθὼν ἐς δέσποιναν ἐμὴν ἀπατήλια βάζει·
sentences.l:
And whoever, wandering, to the land of Ithaca may come,
having gone to my lady, deceits he utters;
sentences.i: And any who comes wandering to the land of Ithaca goes to my lady and tells deceitful tales;
sentences.n: ὃς δέ κ’ is ὃς δέ κε: ὅς κε with the subjunctive ἵκηται ‘may come’ is a general relative, ‘whoever’. ἀλητεύων is ‘going about as a vagrant’. δῆμος is ‘land, countryside’ (house ‘land’). δέσποιναν ἐμήν is ‘my lady’, the wife of the absent master mentioned at 123. ἀπατήλια is the neuter plural of ἀπατήλιος ‘deceitful’ used as a noun, ‘deceits’, and βάζει is ‘utters’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ εὖ δεξαμένη φιλέει καὶ ἕκαστα μεταλλᾷ,
καί οἱ ὀδυρομένῃ βλεφάρων ἄπο δάκρυα πίπτει,
ἣ θέμις ἐστὶ γυναικός, ἐπὴν πόσις ἄλλοθ’ ὄληται.
sentences.l:
and she, having received him well, welcomes him and asks about each thing,
and to her, lamenting, from her eyelids tears fall,
which is the custom of a woman, when her husband elsewhere has perished.
sentences.i: and she receives him well, welcomes him and asks about every detail, and tears fall from her eyelids as she weeps, as is the custom of a woman when her husband has died elsewhere.
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, the pronoun. εὖ δεξαμένη is the aorist middle participle ‘having received (him) well’. φιλέει is the uncontracted φιλεῖ, ‘welcomes’ here, and μεταλλᾷ is μεταλλάει ‘asks about’, with ἕκαστα ‘each thing, every detail’. οἱ ὀδυρομένῃ is ‘to her, as she laments’, the dative of the person affected; βλεφάρων ἄπο has ἀπό placed after its noun, ‘from her eyelids’; δάκρυα is neuter plural with a singular verb, πίπτει. ἣ θέμις ἐστί: ἥ is the relative ‘which’, agreeing with θέμις ‘what is customary and right’. ἐπήν is ‘when’, with ἄλλοθ’ (ἄλλοθι ‘elsewhere’) and ὄληται, the aorist middle subjunctive of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’.

sentences.t: αἶψά κε καὶ σύ, γεραιέ, ἔπος παρατεκτήναιο.
sentences.l: Quickly would you too, aged one, fabricate a tale.
sentences.i: You too, old man, would quickly make up a story.
sentences.n: αἶψα is ‘quickly’; κε with the optative παρατεκτήναιο is ‘would’. γεραιέ is the vocative of γεραιός ‘aged’, a form of address different from ὦ γέρον above. ἔπος παρατεκτήναιο: παρατεκταίνομαι is a rare verb built on τέκτων ‘builder’; ‘fabricate, make up’ is the sense given for it and fits the context. Murray’s full stop ends the unit here, and the condition follows as the next unit.

sentences.t: εἴ τίς τοι χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα δοίη.
sentences.l: If someone to you a cloak and a tunic, clothes, were to give.
sentences.i: If anyone were to give you a cloak and a tunic as clothes.
sentences.n: The unit gives the condition for the one before it. εἰ with the aorist optative δοίη is ‘if anyone were to give’; τοι is ‘to you’. χλαῖνα is the ‘cloak’, a heavy outer wrap, and χιτών the ‘tunic’ worn under it; εἵματα ‘clothes’ stands in apposition to both.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἤδη μέλλουσι κύνες ταχέες τ’ οἰωνοὶ
ῥινὸν ἀπ’ ὀστεόφιν ἐρύσαι, ψυχὴ δὲ λέλοιπεν·
sentences.l:
Of him by now dogs and swift birds are likely
to have drawn the skin from his bones, and the life has left him;
sentences.i: By now the dogs and swift birds must have torn the skin from his bones, and the life has left him;
sentences.n: τοῦ is ‘his’, a genitive pronoun. μέλλουσι with the aorist infinitive ἐρύσαι is ‘are likely to have drawn’; ἤδη is ‘by now’. ταχέες ‘swift’ stands between κύνες and οἰωνοί, and could go with either; l and i attach it to the birds. ῥινόν is ‘skin, hide’; ἀπ’ is ἀπό before its noun; ὀστεόφιν has the ending -φιν, which does the work of a genitive, ‘from the bones’. ἐρύσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἐρύω ‘draw, pull off’. ψυχή is the life that leaves the body; λέλοιπεν is the perfect of λείπω ‘has left’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἢ τόν γ’ ἐν πόντῳ φάγον ἰχθύες, ὀστέα δ’ αὐτοῦ
κεῖται ἐπ’ ἠπείρου ψαμάθῳ εἰλυμένα πολλῇ.
sentences.l:
Or him in the sea the fish ate, and his bones
lie on the mainland, wrapped in much sand.
sentences.i: Or the fish have eaten him in the sea, and his bones lie on the mainland, wrapped in much sand.
sentences.n: ἢ τόν γε is ‘or him, at least’. φάγον is the aorist of ἐσθίω ‘eat’ without the augment, and ἰχθύες is ‘fish’. ὀστέα is neuter plural with the singular verb κεῖται ‘lie’. ἤπειρος is the land as against the sea, ‘the mainland’, as in the previous part; ἐπ’ ἠπείρου is ‘on the mainland’. εἰλυμένα is the perfect passive participle of εἰλύω ‘wrap, enfold’, agreeing with ὀστέα; ψαμάθῳ … πολλῇ is ‘in much sand’, a dative.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὁ μὲν ἔνθ’ ἀπόλωλε, φίλοισι δὲ κήδε’ ὀπίσσω
πᾶσιν, ἐμοὶ δὲ μάλιστα, τετεύχαται·
sentences.l:
So he, there, has perished, and for his friends sorrows hereafter
for all, and for me most of all, have been made ready;
sentences.i: So he has perished there, and sorrows have been prepared for all his friends in time to come, and most of all for me;
sentences.n: ὣς is ‘so, thus’, and ὁ μὲν ἔνθ’ ἀπόλωλε is ‘he, there, has perished’: ἀπόλωλε is the perfect of ἀπόλλυμι. The μέν is answered by δέ in φίλοισι δὲ … ἐμοὶ δὲ μάλιστα. φίλοισι is ‘to friends’, κήδε’ is κήδεα ‘sorrows’, and ὀπίσσω is ‘hereafter, in time to come’. τετεύχαται is the perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make, prepare’: the sorrows ‘have been made ready’. The unit ends at the ano teleia, mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἄλλον
ἤπιον ὧδε ἄνακτα κιχήσομαι, ὁππόσ’ ἐπέλθω,
οὐδ’ εἴ κεν πατρὸς καὶ μητέρος αὖτις ἵκωμαι
οἶκον, ὅθι πρῶτον γενόμην καί μ’ ἔτρεφον αὐτοί.
sentences.l:
for no longer another
lord so kind shall I find, to whatever place I go,
not even if, of father and of mother, again I come to
the house, where first I was born and they themselves reared me.
sentences.i: I shall not find another lord so gentle, wherever I may go, not even if I came back again to the house of my father and mother, where I was first born and they themselves brought me up.
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἄλλον is ‘for no other any more’. ἤπιον is ‘kind’ (‘gentle’ in i); ἄνακτα is ‘lord’; κιχήσομαι is the future of κιχάνω ‘find, come upon’. ὁππόσ’ is read here as ὁππόσε ‘to whatever place’, elided, with ἐπέλθω the aorist subjunctive of ἐπέρχομαι ‘go to’; the form could also be ὁππόσα, ‘as many as’. οὐδ’ εἴ κεν … ἵκωμαι is ‘not even if I should come’, with πατρὸς καὶ μητέρος ‘of father and mother’ and the object οἶκον ‘house’ set on the next line. γενόμην is the aorist ‘I was born’ without the augment, and ἔτρεφον is ‘reared’, with αὐτοί ‘themselves’, the parents.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ νυ τῶν ἔτι τόσσον ὀδύρομαι, ἱέμενός περ
ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδέσθαι ἐὼν ἐν πατρίδι γαίῃ·
sentences.l:
And for them I no longer lament so much, though eager
with my eyes to see them, being in my fatherland;
sentences.i: And I do not grieve for them so much any more, though I long to see them with my eyes in my fatherland;
sentences.n: τῶν is a pronoun, ‘for them’, the genitive object of ὀδύρομαι ‘lament for’, and means the parents just named; νυ is a weak particle. ἔτι is ‘any longer’, τόσσον ‘so much’. ἱέμενος περ is ‘though eager’, περ giving the concessive sense. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδέσθαι is ‘to see with the eyes’, the infinitive being the aorist middle of ὁράω. ἐὼν is ὤν ‘being’. πατρίδι γαίῃ is the house ‘fatherland’, with the Ionic dative -ῃ where Attic has γῇ. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀλλά μ’ Ὀδυσσῆος πόθος αἴνυται οἰχομένοιο.
sentences.l: but me for Odysseus longing seizes, who is gone.
sentences.i: but it is longing for Odysseus, who is gone, that takes hold of me.
sentences.n: μ’ is με. Ὀδυσσῆος is the Homeric genitive of Ὀδυσσεύς, and πόθος Ὀδυσσῆος is ‘longing for Odysseus’. αἴνυται is ‘takes, seizes’. οἰχομένοιο is the genitive participle of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’, agreeing with Ὀδυσσῆος; -οιο is the old ending of the genitive, Attic -ου.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγών, ὦ ξεῖνε, καὶ οὐ παρεόντ’ ὀνομάζειν
αἰδέομαι·
sentences.l:
Him, I, O stranger, even when he is not here, to name
am ashamed;
sentences.i: Stranger, I shrink from naming him, even when he is not here;
sentences.n: τόν is a pronoun, ‘him’, the object of ὀνομάζειν ‘to name’. ἐγών is ἐγώ. ὦ ξεῖνε is ‘O stranger’, spoken to Odysseus. καὶ οὐ παρεόντ’ is ‘even when he is not present’, παρεόντα being the participle of πάρειμι agreeing with τόν. αἰδέομαι is the verb of αἰδώς: ‘I am ashamed of, I feel awe at’; the sense is that he will not use the name lightly. The unit ends at the ano teleia, after the first word of line 146.

sentences.t: πέρι γάρ μ’ ἐφίλει καὶ κήδετο θυμῷ·
sentences.l: for beyond all he loved me and cared for me in his heart;
sentences.i: for he loved me above all and cared for me in his heart;
sentences.n: πέρι is the adverb ‘exceedingly, above all’; γάρ μ’ is γάρ με. ἐφίλει is the imperfect of φιλέω, ‘loved’ here, and κήδετο the imperfect of κήδομαι ‘care for’. θυμῷ is ‘in his heart’, the dative of where the feeling lies. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀλλά μιν ἠθεῖον καλέω καὶ νόσφιν ἐόντα.
sentences.l: but him I call honoured one, even when he is far away.”
sentences.i: but I call him my honoured one, even though he is far away.”
sentences.n: μιν is ‘him’. ἠθεῖος is a word of affection or respect, but its exact sense is not known; ‘honoured one’ is a guess from the dictionary glosses ‘dear, honoured’. καλέω is the uncontracted καλῶ ‘I call’. καὶ νόσφιν ἐόντα is ‘even being far off’: ἐόντα is ὄντα, agreeing with μιν, and νόσφιν is ‘apart, afar’. This ends Eumaeus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Odysseus now replies. The formula is τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ‘then he addressed him in turn’: αὖτε is ‘in turn, again’ and προσέειπε the aorist ‘addressed’. πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ (πολύ- ‘much’ and the root of τλάω ‘endure’) and δῖος ‘heavenly’ are stock epithets, both translated every time with the name.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐπειδὴ πάμπαν ἀναίνεαι, οὐδ’ ἔτι φῇσθα
κεῖνον ἐλεύσεσθαι, θυμὸς δέ τοι αἰὲν ἄπιστος·
sentences.l:
“O friend, since utterly you refuse, and no longer say
that he will come, and your heart is always unbelieving;
sentences.i: “My friend, since you flatly refuse and no longer say that he will come, and your heart is always unbelieving;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλ’ is ὦ φίλε ‘my friend’. ἐπειδή is ‘since’; ἀναίνεαι is ‘you refuse (to believe)’, and πάμπαν ‘altogether’. οὐδ’ ἔτι φῇσθα: φῇσθα is the second person of φημί with the ending -σθα (Attic φῇς), ‘you say’, so ‘you no longer say’; its infinitive is ἐλεύσεσθαι, the future of ἔρχομαι, ‘that he will come’, with κεῖνον ‘that man’. θυμὸς δέ τοι αἰὲν ἄπιστος has no verb: τοι is ‘your’ (the dative of the possessor), αἰέν is αἰεί ‘always’, and ἄπιστος is ‘unbelieving’ (ἀ- ‘not’ and πίστις). The main clause comes with ἀλλ’ ἐγώ in the next lines.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ αὔτως μυθήσομαι, ἀλλὰ σὺν ὅρκῳ,
ὡς νεῖται Ὀδυσεύς·
sentences.l:
But I not just so will speak, but with an oath,
that Odysseus is coming home;
sentences.i: But I will not say it without more ado, but with an oath, that Odysseus is on his way home;
sentences.n: αὔτως is ‘just so, without more ado’; μυθήσομαι is the future of μυθέομαι ‘tell, say’. σὺν ὅρκῳ is ‘with an oath’: the oath follows in lines 158 and 159. ὡς is ‘that’, introducing what he swears; νεῖται is νέεται, from νέομαι ‘go, come back’, a present with the sense of a future, ‘is coming’. Ὀδυσεύς has a single sigma, a metrical variant of Ὀδυσσεύς. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
εὐαγγέλιον δέ μοι ἔστω
αὐτίκ’, ἐπεί κεν κεῖνος ἰὼν τὰ ἃ δώμαθ’ ἵκηται·
sentences.l:
and a reward for good news for me let there be
at once, when that man, going, to his own halls shall come;
sentences.i: and let me have my reward for the good news at once, as soon as he comes to his own halls;
sentences.n: εὐαγγέλιον is the reward given to the bringer of good news, not the news itself: ‘reward for good news’. ἔστω is the third-person imperative ‘let there be’, and μοι ‘for me’. αὐτίκ’ is ‘at once’. ἐπεί κεν … ἵκηται is ‘as soon as he shall come’, ἵκηται being the aorist subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι, with ἰών ‘going’. τὰ ἃ δώμαθ’: τά is the article, ἃ is the possessive ‘his own’ (ἑός, neuter plural), not a relative, and δώμαθ’ is δώματα ‘halls’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἕσσαι με χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε, εἵματα καλά·
sentences.l: to clothe me in cloak and tunic, fine clothes;
sentences.i: namely, that you clothe me in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothes;
sentences.n: ἕσσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, and it says what the reward is to be: ‘to clothe me’. χλαῖνάν and χιτῶνα are the ‘cloak’ and ‘tunic’ as above, and εἵματα καλά ‘fine clothes’ stands in apposition to them. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: πρὶν δέ κε, καὶ μάλα περ κεχρημένος, οὔ τι δεχοίμην.
sentences.l: But before that, even though very much in need, I would in no way accept.
sentences.i: But before then, however great my need, I would accept nothing.
sentences.n: πρίν is ‘before’ (that time). κε with the optative δεχοίμην is ‘I would accept’, and οὔ τι ‘in no way’; the thing refused, the clothes, is left unsaid. καὶ μάλα περ κεχρημένος is ‘even though very much in need’: περ gives the concessive force, and κεχρημένος ‘needing’ is the participle already seen at 124.

sentences.t:
ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσι
γίγνεται, ὃς πενίῃ εἴκων ἀπατήλια βάζει.
sentences.l:
For hateful to me that man, just like the gates of Hades,
becomes, who, yielding to poverty, utters deceits.
sentences.i: For that man is as hateful to me as the gates of Hades, who gives way to poverty and tells deceitful tales.
sentences.n: ἐχθρός is ‘hateful’ and κεῖνος ‘that man’, the one described by ὃς … βάζει in the next line. ὁμῶς with the dative is ‘equally with, just like’; Ἀΐδαο is the genitive of Ἀΐδης (Hades) in -αο, and πύλῃσι ‘gates’ is a dative plural: the gates of Hades are the figure for what is hated. γίγνεται is ‘becomes’. πενίῃ εἴκων is ‘yielding to poverty’ (εἴκω with the dative). ἀπατήλια βάζει is the phrase of 127.

sentences.t:
ἴστω νῦν Ζεὺς πρῶτα θεῶν, ξενίη τε τράπεζα,
ἱστίη τ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος, ἣν ἀφικάνω·
sentences.l:
Let Zeus now know, first of the gods, and the table of hospitality,
and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come;
sentences.i: Let Zeus now know, first of the gods, and the table of hospitality, and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come;
sentences.n: The oath. ἴστω is the third-person imperative of οἶδα ‘know’; calling a power to ‘know’ is calling it to witness. πρῶτα θεῶν is ‘first of the gods’. ξενίη τράπεζα is ‘the table of hospitality’, the table at which a guest is received; ξενίη may be a noun or a feminine adjective, with the same sense. ἱστίη is the Ionic form of Attic ἑστία ‘hearth’; Ὀδυσῆος has one sigma, a metrical variant. ἀμύμονος is ‘blameless’ by the house rendering, though the real meaning of ἀμύμων is not known. ἣν ἀφικάνω: ἥν is the relative, ‘to which’ (the hearth), and ἀφικάνω is a present ‘I come to’, a lengthened form of ἀφικνέομαι.

sentences.t: ἦ μέν τοι τάδε πάντα τελείεται ὡς ἀγορεύω.
sentences.l: Truly to you all these things will be fulfilled, as I say.
sentences.i: All this will truly come about, just as I say.
sentences.n: ἦ μέν is ‘truly’, strengthening the oath. τοι is ‘to you’, or the particle ‘I assure you’; l takes the dative. τελείεται is a present passive of τελέω ‘fulfil’ with the sense of a future, ‘will be fulfilled’. ὡς ἀγορεύω is ‘as I say’.

sentences.t: τοῦδ’ αὐτοῦ λυκάβαντος ἐλεύσεται ἐνθάδ’ Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l: Within this very year will come here Odysseus.
sentences.i: Within this very year Odysseus will come here.
sentences.n: λυκάβας is a word whose meaning is not known; ‘year’ is the traditional guess, and the next line gives the date more closely. The genitive τοῦδ’ αὐτοῦ λυκάβαντος means ‘within this very (period)’. ἐλεύσεται is the future of ἔρχομαι, and ἐνθάδ’ is ‘here’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένοιο,
οἴκαδε νοστήσει, καὶ τίσεται ὅς τις ἐκείνου
ἐνθάδ’ ἀτιμάζει ἄλοχον καὶ φαίδιμον υἱόν.
sentences.l:
As the one month wanes and the other begins,
he will return home, and will take vengeance on whoever of that man
here dishonours the wife and glorious son.”
sentences.i: At the turn of the month, as one wanes and the next begins, he will come home, and he will punish whoever here dishonours his wife and his glorious son.”
sentences.n: τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘the one month waning, the other beginning’, that is at the change of month; φθίνοντος is ‘waning’ (φθίνω) and ἱσταμένοιο ‘beginning’ (ἵσταμαι), with -οιο for -ου. οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’ (the suffix -δε gives direction), and νοστήσει the future of νοστέω ‘return home’. τίσεται is the future middle of τίνυμαι ‘take vengeance on’; ὅς τις is ‘whoever’. ἐκείνου ‘of that man’ goes with both ἄλοχον ‘wife’ and υἱόν ‘son’, and φαίδιμον ‘glorious’ is the house rendering.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: Here the poet turns and speaks to Eumaeus as ‘you’. ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’ and προσέφης the second-person aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’. Εὔμαιε and συβῶτα are both vocatives, ‘Eumaeus the swineherd’. The line is a stock formula and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον, οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ἐγὼν εὐαγγέλιον τόδε τίσω,
οὔτ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ἔτι οἶκον ἐλεύσεται·
sentences.l:
“Old man, neither then will I pay this reward for good news,
nor will Odysseus any more come home;
sentences.i: “Old man, I shall not pay this reward for good news, and Odysseus will not come home any more;
sentences.n: οὔτ’ … οὔτ’ is ‘neither … nor’, and ἄρ’ is the particle ‘then’. ἐγών is ἐγώ. εὐαγγέλιον τόδε is ‘this reward for good news’, the reward Odysseus asked for at 152; τίσω is the future of τίνω ‘pay’. οἶκον ἐλεύσεται is ‘will come to the house’, with ἔτι ‘any more’. The unit ends at the ano teleia, before ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος
πῖνε, καὶ ἄλλα παρὲξ μεμνώμεθα, μηδέ με τούτων
μίμνησκ’·
sentences.i: but drink at ease, and let us turn our thoughts to other things, and do not remind me of these;
sentences.n: ἀλλά is ‘but’, ἕκηλος ‘at ease’, and πῖνε the imperative ‘drink’. μεμνώμεθα is the perfect subjunctive of μιμνήσκω (perfect μέμνημαι ‘have in mind’), a ‘let us’ form, with ἄλλα παρέξ ‘other things apart (from these)’. μηδέ με τούτων μίμνησκ’: μίμνησκ’ is the elided imperative ‘remind’, which takes the genitive of the thing, τούτων ‘of these’. The unit ends at the ano teleia, after the first word of line 169.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐμοῖσιν
ἄχνυται, ὁππότε τις μνήσῃ κεδνοῖο ἄνακτος.
sentences.l:
for truly the heart in my breast
grieves, whenever anyone mentions a trusty lord.
sentences.i: for my heart grieves in my breast whenever anyone mentions my trusty lord.
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’. ἐνί is ἐν ‘in’; στήθεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσιν, ‘breast’; ἐμοῖσιν is the dative plural of ἐμός ‘my’. ἄχνυται is ‘grieves’. ὁππότε τις μνήσῃ is ‘whenever anyone mentions’, μνήσῃ being the aorist subjunctive of μιμνήσκω, the verb of μίμνησκ’ above, here with the genitive. κεδνοῖο ἄνακτος is ‘a trusty lord’: κεδνός is ‘trusty’ by the house rendering, ἄναξ is ‘lord’, and -οιο is the old genitive ending.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι ὅρκον μὲν ἐάσομεν, αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἔλθοι ὅπως μιν ἐγώ γ’ ἐθέλω καὶ Πηνελόπεια
Λαέρτης θ’ ὁ γέρων καὶ Τηλέμαχος θεοειδής.
sentences.l:
But truly the oath we will let be, but Odysseus
may he come as I for my part wish, and Penelope,
and Laertes the old man, and Telemachus godlike-in-form.
sentences.i: But let us leave the oath alone, and may Odysseus come as I wish, and Penelope, and old Laertes, and Telemachus, godlike in form.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι is ‘but truly’. ἐάσομεν is the first person plural of ἐάω ‘let be, let alone’, a future or a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘we will leave’. ὅρκον μὲν is answered by αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεύς ‘but Odysseus’. ἔλθοι is the optative of wish, ‘may he come’, and ὅπως μιν ἐγώ γ’ ἐθέλω is ‘as I, for my part, wish him (to)’; the others who wish it are added by καί: Penelope, Laertes the old man (ὁ γέρων, the article with the noun) and Telemachus. θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’ (θεός and εἶδος ‘form’), the house rendering.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ παιδὸς ἄλαστον ὀδύρομαι, ὃν τέκ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
Τηλεμάχου·
sentences.l:
Now in turn for a son, unforgettably, I lament, whom Odysseus begot,
Telemachus;
sentences.i: Now I mourn in turn, past forgetting, for a son, Telemachus, whom Odysseus fathered;
sentences.n: νῦν αὖ is ‘now in turn’: Eumaeus turns from the father to the son. παιδός is the genitive after ὀδύρομαι ‘lament for’, and Τηλεμάχου, in the same case, names him. ἄλαστον is an adverb whose meaning is not certain: dictionaries tie it to λήθω ‘forget’, ‘not to be forgotten’, but ‘unceasing’ and ‘grievous’ are also given. ὃν τέκ’ Ὀδυσσεύς: ὅν is the relative ‘whom’, not the possessive ‘his own’, and τέκ’ is the elided τέκε, ἔτεκε ‘begot’ without its augment. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τὸν ἐπεὶ θρέψαν θεοὶ ἔρνεϊ ἶσον,
καί μιν ἔφην ἔσσεσθαι ἐν ἀνδράσιν οὔ τι χέρηα
πατρὸς ἑοῖο φίλοιο, δέμας καὶ εἶδος ἀγητόν,
sentences.l:
Him, when the gods had reared him equal to a sapling,
and I said he would be among men in no way worse
than his own dear father, in body and form admirable,
sentences.i: The gods reared him like a young sapling, and I said that among men he would be no worse than his own dear father, admirable in body and form,
sentences.n: τόν is a pronoun, ‘him’, Telemachus. θρέψαν is the aorist of τρέφω ‘rear’, unaugmented, with the ending -αν. ἔρνεϊ ἶσον is ‘equal to a sapling’, ἔρνος being a young shoot. ἔφην is ‘I said’, ἔσσεσθαι the future infinitive of εἰμί; οὔ τι χέρηα is ‘in no way worse’ (χέρης ‘inferior’). πατρὸς ἑοῖο φίλοιο is the genitive of comparison, ‘than his own dear father’: ἑοῖο is the possessive ‘his own’, φίλοιο ‘dear’. δέμας καὶ εἶδος ἀγητόν: δέμας ‘body’ and εἶδος ‘form’ are accusatives of respect, and ἀγητόν ‘admirable’ agrees with μιν. The sentence breaks off at the comma and begins again in the next unit with τὸν δέ.

sentences.t:
τὸν δέ τις ἀθανάτων βλάψε φρένας ἔνδον ἐΐσας
ἠέ τις ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.l:
But him some one of the immortals harmed, his balanced wits within,
or some one of men;
sentences.i: but one of the immortals harmed his well-balanced wits, or else one of mankind;
sentences.n: τὸν δέ is ‘but him’, still Telemachus; τις ἀθανάτων is ‘some one of the immortals’. βλάψε is the aorist of βλάπτω ‘harm’, without the augment. φρένας ἔνδον ἐΐσας is ‘his wits within, balanced’: φρένες are the mind, ἔνδον is ‘within’, and ἐΐσας is the accusative plural of ἐΐσος ‘equal, even’, a stock epithet of φρένες; ‘balanced’ is the traditional reading and is not certain. ἠέ is ‘or’; τις ἀνθρώπων is ‘some one of men’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἔβη μετὰ πατρὸς ἀκουὴν
ἐς Πύλον ἠγαθέην·
sentences.l:
and he went, in quest of news of his father,
to holy Pylos;
sentences.i: and he went off to holy Pylos in search of news of his father;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’, Telemachus. ἔβη is the aorist of βαίνω ‘went’. μετὰ πατρὸς ἀκουήν is ‘after news of his father’: μετά with the accusative is ‘in pursuit of’, and ἀκουή is ‘a hearing, report’. ἠγαθέην is a stock epithet of Pylos, rendered ‘holy’ by the house rule. The unit ends at the ano teleia, mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοὶ
οἴκαδ’ ἰόντα λοχῶσιν, ὅπως ἀπὸ φῦλον ὄληται
νώνυμον ἐξ Ἰθάκης Ἀρκεισίου ἀντιθέοιο.
sentences.l:
And him the noble suitors
as he goes home lie in ambush for, so that utterly may perish the race
nameless, out of Ithaca, of godlike Arcesius.
sentences.i: and the noble suitors are lying in ambush for him as he goes home, so that the race of godlike Arcesius may perish out of Ithaca, nameless.
sentences.n: τὸν δέ is ‘and him’, the pronoun again. μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί ‘the noble suitors’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. οἴκαδ’ ἰόντα is ‘as he goes home’: οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’, and ἰόντα is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’, agreeing with τόν. λοχῶσιν is the contracted form of λοχάω ‘lie in ambush for’. ὅπως … ὄληται is a purpose clause; ἀπὸ … ὄληται is a tmesis for ἀπόληται ‘may perish utterly’, with φῦλον ‘race, tribe’ as subject. νώνυμον is ‘nameless’ (without a name, so unremembered). Ἀρκεισίου ἀντιθέοιο is ‘of godlike Arcesius’, ἀντίθεος being ‘godlike’; he is named only here in this part, and his ‘race’ is the family line the suitors would end.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι κεῖνον μὲν ἐάσομεν, ἤ κεν ἁλώῃ
ἦ κε φύγῃ καί κέν οἱ ὑπέρσχῃ χεῖρα Κρονίων.
sentences.l:
But truly him we will let be, whether he is caught
or escapes, and the son of Cronus may hold his hand over him.
sentences.i: But we will leave him be, whether he is caught or escapes, and the son of Cronus may hold his hand over him.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι κεῖνον μὲν ἐάσομεν has the same shape as 171, ‘we will let him be’; κεῖνον now means Telemachus, where it meant Odysseus at 150. ἤ κεν ἁλώῃ ἦ κε φύγῃ is ‘whether he is caught or escapes’: ἁλώῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be captured’ (active in form, passive in sense), φύγῃ the aorist subjunctive of φεύγω. καί κέν οἱ ὑπέρσχῃ χεῖρα is ‘and he may hold his hand over him’: ὑπέρσχῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ὑπερέχω, and holding a hand over someone is the figure for protecting him. Κρονίων is ‘the son of Cronus’, that is Zeus, named here by his patronymic only.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι σύ, γεραιέ, τὰ σ’ αὐτοῦ κήδε’ ἐνίσπες
καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῶ·
sentences.l:
But come, tell me, you, aged one, your own sorrows,
and tell me this truly, so that I may know it well:
sentences.i: But come, old man, tell me your own sorrows, and tell me this truly, so that I may know it well:
sentences.n: Eumaeus now turns to the stranger and asks for his story. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, with ἄγε the imperative of ἄγω used as an interjection; μοι is ‘for me’ and σύ ‘you’, emphatic; γεραιέ is ‘aged one’ as at 131. τὰ σ’ αὐτοῦ κήδε’ is τὰ σά … αὐτοῦ κήδεα, ‘your own sorrows’; ἐνίσπες is the aorist imperative of ἐνέπω ‘tell’. In the second line ἀγόρευσον is the aorist imperative of ἀγορεύω, ἐτήτυμον ‘truly’, and ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῶ ‘so that I may know well’, with the subjunctive of οἶδα. The second line is a stock line, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.l: Who among men are you, and from where?
sentences.i: Who among men are you, and where from?
sentences.n: τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν: εἶς is ‘you are’ (the second person of εἰμί), and ἀνδρῶν is ‘among men’, a partitive genitive. πόθεν is ‘from where’, the suffix -θεν giving the place from which. This is a stock question, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: πόθι τοι πόλις ἠδὲ τοκῆες;
sentences.l: Where is your city and your parents?
sentences.i: Where is your city, and where are your parents?
sentences.n: πόθι is ‘where’, the suffix -θι giving place at which, against πόθεν in the question before. τοι is ‘your’, the dative of the possessor; πόλις is ‘city’ and ἠδέ ‘and’; τοκῆες are ‘parents’.

sentences.t: ὁπποίης τ’ ἐπὶ νηὸς ἀφίκεο·
sentences.l: And on what sort of ship did you come?
sentences.i: And on what kind of ship did you come?
sentences.n: ὁπποίης … νηός is ‘of what kind of ship’: ὁποῖος, properly an indirect-question word, is used here in a direct question, with νηός the genitive of ναῦς ‘ship’ and ἐπί ‘on’ standing before it; τ’ is τε ‘and’. ἀφίκεο is the aorist second person of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive’, with -εο for -ου. Murray ends the clause with an ano teleia, mid-line, though the sense is a question like those on either side of it, and the English closes it as a question.

sentences.t:
πῶς δέ σε ναῦται
ἤγαγον εἰς Ἰθάκην;
sentences.l:
and how did sailors
bring you to Ithaca?
sentences.i: And how did sailors bring you to Ithaca?
sentences.n: πῶς is ‘how’; σε ‘you’; ναῦται ‘sailors’; ἤγαγον is the aorist of ἄγω ‘bring’, and εἰς Ἰθάκην is ‘to Ithaca’ (εἰς is the same word as ἐς). The unit ends at the Greek question mark, mid-line.

sentences.t: τίνες ἔμμεναι εὐχετόωντο;
sentences.l: Who did they declare themselves to be?
sentences.i: Who did they declare themselves to be?
sentences.n: τίνες is ‘who’, plural, the sailors. ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί ‘to be’ (Attic εἶναι). εὐχετόωντο is the imperfect of εὐχετάομαι ‘declare, claim’ (the house ‘declare’ of εὔχομαι with an infinitive), with the open vowels -όω- of diectasis, where Attic would contract to -ῶντο.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τί σε πεζὸν ὀΐομαι ἐνθάδ’ ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l: For in no way do I suppose that you came here on foot.”
sentences.i: For I do not at all suppose that you came here on foot.”
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τί σε: οὐ … τί (with μέν ‘indeed’ and γάρ between them) is ‘in no way’, and σε ‘you’ is the subject of the infinitive. πεζόν is ‘on foot’, an adjective used as a predicate with σε, and ὀΐομαι is ‘I think, suppose’. ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’, and ἐνθάδ’ is ‘here’. The point of the questions is that he must have come by ship, hence the questions about the ship and the sailors. This ends Eumaeus’ speech. The English repeats that of the identical line published in the first part, where the speech runs on; only the closing quotation mark is added.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς
τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι ταῦτα μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.l:
Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
“Well then, I will tell you these things very exactly.
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him: “Then I will tell you all of this quite exactly.
sentences.n: The reply-formula: ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is ‘answering, addressed’. πολύμητις is ‘of many wiles’ (πολύ- ‘many’ and μῆτις ‘cunning intelligence’), a stock epithet of Odysseus, translated every time. τοιγάρ is ‘well then, therefore’; ἐγώ τοι is ‘I … to you’, with τοι the dative ‘to you’. ταῦτα is ‘these things’, and ἀτρεκέως ‘exactly’ with μάλ’ ‘very’. ἀγορεύσω is a future, or a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘I will tell’. The line is a stock line, and its English is kept. The source prints no colon at the end of 191; the two lines are one unit here.

sentences.t:
εἴη μὲν νῦν νῶϊν ἐπὶ χρόνον ἠμὲν ἐδωδὴ
ἠδὲ μέθυ γλυκερὸν κλισίης ἔντοσθεν ἐοῦσι,
δαίνυσθαι ἀκέοντ’, ἄλλοι δ’ ἐπὶ ἔργον ἕποιεν·
sentences.i: Now for a time let there be food for the two of us, and sweet wine, here inside the hut, for us to feast in silence, and let the others go to their work;
sentences.n: εἴη is the optative of εἰμί in a wish, ‘may there be’. νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘for us two’, Odysseus and Eumaeus. ἐπὶ χρόνον is ‘for a time’; ἠμὲν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’. ἐδωδή is ‘food’, μέθυ γλυκερόν ‘sweet wine’. κλισίης ἔντοσθεν ἐοῦσι is ‘to us being inside the hut’: κλισίη is a hut or lodge, and ἐοῦσι (= οὖσι) agrees with νῶϊν. δαίνυσθαι ἀκέοντ’ is ‘to feast in silence’, ἀκέοντ’ being elided and agreeing with the two men. ἄλλοι δ’ ἐπὶ ἔργον ἕποιεν is ‘and let others go after their work’: ἕποιεν is the optative of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ῥηϊδίως κεν ἔπειτα καὶ εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν ἅπαντα
οὔ τι διαπρήξαιμι λέγων ἐμὰ κήδεα θυμοῦ,
ὅσσα γε δὴ ξύμπαντα θεῶν ἰότητι μόγησα.
sentences.l:
Easily then, even for a whole year,
not at all could I get through, telling the sorrows of my heart,
as many as all together I have toiled through by the will of the gods.
sentences.i: I could not easily get through the telling of the sorrows of my heart, even in a whole year, all that I have gone through by the will of the gods.
sentences.n: ῥηϊδίως is ‘easily’, and with οὔ τι διαπρήξαιμι the sense is ‘I could not easily get through’. κεν with the optative διαπρήξαιμι is ‘I could’; διαπρήσσω is ‘carry through, finish’. ἔπειτα is ‘then, in that case’. εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν ἅπαντα is ‘for a whole year’. λέγων is ‘telling’, and ἐμὰ κήδεα θυμοῦ ‘the sorrows of my heart’. ὅσσα γε δὴ ξύμπαντα is ‘as many as all together’ (ξύμπαντα = σύμπαντα), and θεῶν ἰότητι ‘by the will of the gods’, with ἰότης ‘will’; μόγησα is the aorist of μογέω ‘toil’. The last line is a stock line, and its English is kept. Odysseus has only begun his answer: the speech goes on into the next part, so no closing quotation mark is set here.
